classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught unitary method by finding a per-item or convenient-group quantity and scaling; the donut part also interprets a two-donut serving.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies proportional scaling to cost, mass or length. Rate problems is the closest catalogue skill; percentages and ratio sharing are not assessed.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1 and 2 scale both quantities together, first dividing to one item or a convenient common unit, then multiplying to the requested quantity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct proportional scaling using a unit quantity or a convenient common unit.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse cost-to-quantity relationships using unitary scaling, with the shares part requiring rounding down because only whole shares can be purchased.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c find quantities from costs, d scales a catering quantity, and e finds pages from words. All directly assess proportional unitary reasoning.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–4 divide to a convenient unit, then multiply to the requested quantity; Example 3 reverses a cost-to-quantity relationship and Example 4 retains exact fractions until the final interpretation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find quantities from proportional costs or amounts, including a non-integral intermediate result and whole-item interpretation.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply proportional scaling to maps, shadows and a recipe.

questions.mappingNote: Each part scales corresponding quantities; parts a–b use map scales, c–d use proportional shadows, and e scales a recipe.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–3 divide corresponding quantities to a convenient unit, then multiply to the required quantity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply proportional scaling to maps, shadows and a recipe.

classification.difficultyReason: Scale a known percentage to another percentage; part c also requires finding the additional number.

questions.mappingNote: The quantities being scaled are percentages; part c asks for the additional 5%, rather than the final holding.
questions.methodNote: Use a convenient common unit as in Examples 2–3, dividing first and then multiplying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Scale a known percentage to another percentage; part c also requires finding the additional number.

classification.difficultyReason: Use unitary calculations with fractional unit costs and a volume conversion.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d apply the unitary method to purchases and composition. Part b follows the exact-cost-then-round sequence of Example 4.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–3 use convenient units; Example 4 retains an exact fractional unit cost until final rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use unitary calculations with fractional unit costs and a volume conversion.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose fractional units and scale amounts, time, workforce or mass.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c use fifths, quarter-hours and sixths of a class; d–e choose convenient fractional amounts before multiplying.
questions.methodNote: Examples 2–3 choose a convenient common unit. The embedded hint extends this approach to fractional units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose fractional units and scale amounts, time, workforce or mass.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare unequal package sizes by finding costs for a common quantity, including recognising equal value.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 applies the taught unitary method to compare prices for equal masses. Best buys is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–4 find a unit quantity by division and then multiply to obtain the required quantity; Example 4 retains exact fractions until rounding is requested.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare unequal package sizes by finding costs for a common quantity, including recognising equal value.

classification.difficultyReason: Scale a packet price to a common mass, then compare prices and calculate the saving.

questions.mappingNote: Use 125 g as the common-factor unit to price 500 g, then compare equal masses. The directly assessed final skill is determining the best buy.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 chooses a common-factor unit, divides to find its cost, then multiplies to find the required quantity. Examples 1 and 4 also demonstrate proportional cost calculations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Scale a packet price to a common mass, then compare prices and calculate the saving.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the time for one journey part, then scale to the four remaining parts.

questions.mappingNote: The question applies the taught divide-then-multiply method to three known journey parts and four remaining parts; unitary-method-ratios is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–3 divide a known quantity into a convenient unit and multiply to obtain the required quantity. Here one seventh of the journey is the convenient unit.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the time for one journey part, then scale to the four remaining parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate rooms, painters and time, recognising that more rooms increase time while more painters decrease it, then scale through painter-hours.

questions.mappingNote: The task coordinates worker count, output and time, so related-rates-problems is the closest supplied catalogue skill. The inspected examples establish unitary scaling but do not explicitly demonstrate inverse worker/time scaling.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–4 reduce a quantity to a convenient unit and then scale to the required quantity. The authored solution applies this sequence to one painter and one room before scaling to four rooms and three painters.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Coordinate the number of painters, rooms and hours by reducing the work to one painter and one room.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the discounted price as 80% of the original and scale back to 100%, following the taught reverse-percentage method.

questions.mappingNote: Part a follows Example 5: 80% to 20% to 100%. Part b follows Example 6a by multiplying the hourly quantity by three. Part c scales 10% to 100%; part d scales 70% to 10% to 100%. Part e finds litres per kilometre before scaling to 200 km. Reverse percentage is the most advanced directly assessed skill in this mixed question.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 identifies the percentage remaining after a discount and scales through a convenient percentage to 100%. Example 6 scales constant-rate quantities through a known unit or convenient intermediate quantity. Page 7 demonstrates successive unit conversions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct applications of the demonstrated unitary method to original prices, whole amounts and constant rates.

classification.difficultyReason: Each part uses a constant rate and a direct unitary calculation.

questions.mappingNote: Part a finds distance per hour; parts b and e find distance per litre; part c finds Australian dollars per US dollar; part d finds minutes lost per month. These directly assess constant-rate problems.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent rates through a one-unit quantity, then multiply by the required quantity. Examples 6 and 8 demonstrate successive rate calculations; retain exact fractions where necessary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Each part uses a constant rate and a direct unitary calculation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover whole quantities from given percentages, identify the surviving percentage, and calculate a remaining quantity with rounding.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b recover a whole from a percentage; c recovers the original amount from 120%; d first identifies the surviving 42%; e identifies the remaining 65% and rounds only the final petrol quantity. Unitary-method-percentages covers the complete task, with reverse-percentage-problems supporting c and d.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 Example 5 identifies the known percentage and scales its value to 100%. Pages 5–6 Example 6 uses successive proportional scaling and exact fractions before converting units. Page 7 Example 8 demonstrates successive one-step conversions. Solutions here scale through 1%, retaining exact fractions until the requested rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover whole quantities from given percentages, identify the surviving percentage, and calculate a remaining quantity with rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate quantity-per-unit relationship and link unit-rate calculations with conversions such as hours to minutes or days to weeks.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b, d and f convert practical rates through a unit rate; c and e simplify quantity-per-unit rates; g finds distance per hour. Rate problems is the closest whole-question skill, supported by rate-unit conversion, simplified rates and speed calculation.
questions.methodNote: Pages 5–6, Example 6, find equivalent quantities and times by dividing and multiplying. Page 7, Changing units and Example 8, demonstrates successive one-step rate conversions. Each solution first finds a quantity per one unit, then scales to the requested unit where necessary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find unit rates and scale them to the requested time or distance units across seven practical contexts.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert compound units and currency using successive unitary steps, including an inverse conversion.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c convert rates to different time or quantity units; d finds distance per litre; e–f use direct and inverse currency rates. Converting rate units is the closest primary skill, supported by practical rate problems.
questions.methodNote: Examples 5 and 6 scale known quantities through convenient unit amounts. Example 8 explicitly teaches successive one-step conversions of both units in a rate. Solutions use these unitary steps and retain exact fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert compound units and currency using successive unitary steps, including an inverse conversion.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate average speed, convert both units of a speed and apply an exchange rate in both directions.

questions.mappingNote: Part a finds distance per hour by division; part b follows successive one-step conversions; parts c i–ii apply the supplied exchange rate directly and inversely. Converting rate units is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue match. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete source task.
questions.methodNote: Examples 5–7 establish equivalent quantities and unitary reasoning. Example 6 finds an unknown time from a constant rate. Page 7 Changing units and Example 8 explicitly teach successive one-step unit conversions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate average speed, convert both units of a speed and apply an exchange rate in both directions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the whole quantity from a known percentage, including a percentage greater than 100.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts recover 100% from a supplied percentage. Part a scales 20% to 10% then 100%; part b scales 110% to 10% then 100%. These directly assess the percentage unitary method.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 finds 100% from a known percentage by dividing to a convenient percentage and multiplying to the whole. Examples 6–8 reinforce successive proportional scaling and unit conversions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover the whole quantity from a known percentage, including a percentage greater than 100.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the taught combined-work method to express both painters' outputs over a common interval, add outputs and convert back to time for one house.

questions.mappingNote: This question explicitly references Example 7 and assesses the same combined-work method with 4-day and 5-day painting times. The common interval is 20 days. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this task.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 on PDF page 6 scales each painter's output to a common number of days, adds their house totals, and divides the common time by the combined number of houses. Pages 5 and 7 establish unitary reasoning and successive equivalent-rate conversions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two different painting rates over a common time interval, then find the time for one house.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly divide the given distance by the given time to obtain average speed in matching units.

questions.mappingNote: Direct calculation of speed from distance and time.
questions.methodNote: Examples 9 and 10 divide distance by time to calculate speed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide distance by a whole-number duration.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly multiply the given speed by the duration to find distance; the units already match.

questions.mappingNote: The unknown is distance for a given speed and duration.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 uses distance = speed × time, alternatively unitary reasoning.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply a speed by a whole-number duration.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly divide distance by speed to obtain journey time with no unit conversion.

questions.mappingNote: Direct calculation of journey time.
questions.methodNote: Examples 12 and 13 calculate time as distance divided by speed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide distance by speed to find time.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the hourly walking distance, explicitly requested in the first part, and reuse it to scale to each duration.

questions.mappingNote: Equivalent constant-speed distances, including a fractional duration.
questions.methodNote: Find the distance in one hour, then multiply by the requested hours, as in the unitary alternatives and Example 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a unit speed and apply it to five durations, including a mixed number.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the car's hourly distance in the first part and multiply that rate by each subsequent duration.

questions.mappingNote: Constant-speed distance calculations.
questions.methodNote: Use the unitary method to find distance in one hour, then multiply by time, retaining fractional arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a constant speed and apply it to five durations.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose speed or distance calculations for a table, including fractional hours.

questions.mappingNote: The table directly assesses the speed–distance–time relationships.
questions.methodNote: Use speed = distance/time for rows a–c and distance = speed × time for rows d–f; keep units consistent with each row.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose speed or distance calculations for a table, including fractional hours.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a mixed hours-and-minutes duration before calculating distance.

questions.mappingNote: Distance calculation with a necessary time conversion.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 converts hours and minutes to a fractional number of hours, then multiplies by speed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a mixed hours-and-minutes duration before calculating distance.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide distance by a mixed-number duration.

questions.mappingNote: Average speed for a single journey.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 calculates speed by dividing distance by fractional hours.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide distance by a mixed-number duration.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert minutes to hours before multiplying by speed.

questions.mappingNote: Distance calculation with minutes converted to hours.
questions.methodNote: Use the consistent-units instruction and distance = speed × time from Example 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert minutes to hours before multiplying by speed.

classification.difficultyReason: Find elapsed time from clock readings and convert to hours.

questions.mappingNote: Elapsed time is an intermediate step in a distance calculation.
questions.methodNote: Apply distance = speed × time after expressing the elapsed time in hours, following Example 11 and the unit-consistency warning.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find elapsed time from clock readings and convert to hours.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate stage speeds and use total distance over total time for a two-stage journey.

questions.mappingNote: Part d directly assesses whole-journey average speed; earlier parts provide total time and stage calculations.
questions.methodNote: The average-speed definition uses distance travelled divided by time taken. Apply it separately to stages and to the complete journey, retaining exact fractional hours as in Example 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate stage speeds and use total distance over total time for a two-stage journey.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine three distances and durations, convert units, then calculate average speed over the event.

questions.mappingNote: Whole-event average speed across three disciplines is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use average speed = distance travelled/time taken across the complete event; heed the consistent-units warning on page 12 and retain exact fractional arithmetic as in Example 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine three distances and durations, convert units, then calculate average speed over the event.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate distances and times for two swimming stages, convert minutes to seconds and combine the stages while excluding the rest.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply distance divided by time in metres and seconds. Part c applies the same definition to the combined swimming distance and combined swimming time, with the explicitly excluded rest omitted.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines speed as distance divided by time. Page 10 distinguishes average speed and demonstrates formula and unitary methods in Examples 9–10. Pages 11–12 develop distance and time calculations and require consistent units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate distances and times for two swimming stages, convert minutes to seconds and combine the stages while excluding the rest.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the total journey time, convert the fractional hour to minutes and determine the arrival time.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the taught time formula to the full 422 km journey, convert the fractional hour to minutes and add the journey time to 8 a.m. The supplied 320 km remains in the prompt.
questions.methodNote: Examples 12 and 13 calculate time by dividing distance by speed. Example 13 converts a fractional hour to minutes; the Speed summary requires consistent units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate the total journey time, convert the fractional hour to minutes and determine the arrival time.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the distances covered in each second by two runners approaching one another, then calculate the meeting time.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is finding time from distance and speed. Combining the two contributions to gap closure extends the inspected unitary method; these pages contain no explicit worked meeting-runners example.
questions.methodNote: Pages 9–10 interpret speed as distance covered per unit time. Examples 12–13 on pages 11–12 calculate time by dividing distance by the distance covered in one time unit. Here the runners together close 4 + 6 = 10 metres of the gap each second, so 120 metres takes 12 seconds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine the distances covered in each second by two runners approaching one another, then calculate the meeting time.

classification.difficultyReason: Write ordered ratios directly from two given counts, adding the counts for the whole.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b compare the two category counts in opposite orders; part c compares oranges with the total count, exactly as in Example 14. All three ratios already have HCF 1.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 writes category counts in the requested order and adds both counts before forming a category-to-total ratio. Page 17 explains simplification by dividing all terms by their HCF.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Write ordered ratios directly from two given counts, adding the counts for the whole.

classification.difficultyReason: Count shapes and coloured subsets, then divide both terms by their highest common factor.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts require ordered counts from the shape diagram and simplest whole-number ratios, so simplify-ratios is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 preserves the requested comparison order; the ribbon models establish counting equal parts. Page 17 teaches reduction by dividing every ratio term by the HCF.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count shapes and coloured subsets, then divide both terms by their highest common factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Forms and simplifies a two-part ratio of volumes already expressed in millilitres.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 uses the same mixture method with 100 mL of pure orange juice and 900 mL of water; the assessed result is a simplified same-unit ratio.
questions.methodNote: Example 15 takes one part as 100 mL and expresses each volume as a number of these equal parts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Forms and simplifies a two-part ratio of volumes already expressed in millilitres.

classification.difficultyReason: Add the two ratio parts and express each category as a fraction of their total.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess expressing a category as a fraction of the whole from a part-to-part ratio.
questions.methodNote: Example 16 on PDF page 16 adds the ratio parts to find the whole, then writes each category's parts over that total.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add the two ratio parts and express each category as a fraction of their total.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the given fraction to identify one blue part and two other-coloured parts.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies the same fraction-to-part-ratio method to blue flowers and all other-coloured flowers.
questions.methodNote: Example 17 on PDF page 16 subtracts the given fraction from one, then compares the numbers of equal parts belonging to the named group and the rest.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the given fraction to identify one blue part and two other-coloured parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Add two ratio terms and express each piece as a fraction of the whole.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess expressing a ratio part as a fraction of the whole. The source ratio is 1:2, so the shorter and longer pieces contain 1 and 2 of the 3 total parts respectively. The offered rope reuse candidate has ratio 3:2 and is not source-identical.
questions.methodNote: The ribbon explanation on page 15 and Examples 16 and 18 add the ratio terms to find the total number of equal parts, then express each required part over that total.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add two ratio terms and express each piece as a fraction of the whole.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a given fraction into equal parts and compare the green part with the remaining blue parts.

questions.mappingNote: One-fifth green gives one green part and four blue parts, directly applying Example 17's fraction-to-ratio method.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 introduces equal parts. Example 17 on page 16 converts a fraction of a population into a part-to-remainder ratio by dividing the whole into equal parts and counting the remaining parts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a given fraction into equal parts and compare the green part with the remaining blue parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the complementary female fraction and translate the male and female shares into an ordered part-to-part ratio.

questions.mappingNote: Apply Example 17 to two-sevenths male: the remaining five-sevenths are female, giving male:female = 2:5.
questions.methodNote: Example 17 on PDF page 16 subtracts the given fraction from 1, then compares equal parts to express the specified group to the rest as a ratio. Page 15 connects ratios with fractions; pages 17–18 develop simplification and ratios of fractional quantities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the remaining fraction and compare the numbers of equal parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide both whole-number terms by their highest common factor.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses simplifying a two-term whole-number ratio by a common factor; no unit conversion or fraction elimination is required.
questions.methodNote: The explanation and Example 19 on PDF page 17 reduce whole-number ratios by dividing every term by the highest common factor. Pages 15–16 establish equal parts; page 18 distinguishes eliminating fractions before simplification.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide both whole-number terms by their highest common factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Subtract male students from the total before forming and simplifying the male-to-female ratio, then distinguish that comparison from the male fraction of the whole.

questions.mappingNote: Part a combines finding the remaining population with HCF simplification. Part b directly assesses expressing a component population as a fraction of the whole.
questions.methodNote: Examples 16 and 18 express a component as a fraction of the whole. Example 17 finds the remaining population by subtraction. Page 17 teaches simplifying ratios by dividing every term by the highest common factor. The exercise instruction on page 18 requires ratios in simplest form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the complementary population, simplify its comparison ratio, and express the male population as a fraction of the whole.

classification.difficultyReason: Place the supplied counts in the requested order and divide both ratio terms by their common factor.

questions.mappingNote: This question compares the given CD and DVD counts, then simplifies 27:60 by dividing both terms by 3. Simplifying whole-number ratios is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 models writing quantities in the requested ratio order. Page 17 teaches dividing all ratio terms by their highest common factor, illustrated in Example 19. Page 18 supplies the exercise-wide instruction to express all ratios in simplest form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Write the two counts in the requested order and divide both terms by their highest common factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught common-denominator procedure to express the three ingredient fractions as whole-number ratio terms.

questions.mappingNote: Question 12 directly applies Example 20 to fractional volumes of three ingredients. Multiplication by 8 gives the simplest whole-number ratio 3:4:1.
questions.methodNote: Pages 15–16 introduce equal parts and ratios of multiple quantities. Page 17 instructs multiplying fractional ratio terms by their lowest common denominator. Example 20 on page 18 demonstrates converting three fractional mixture quantities to a whole-number ratio.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express three fractional volumes as whole-number ratio terms using their lowest common denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear fractional or decimal terms by common multiplication, then reduce the resulting whole-number ratio.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess simplifying ratios containing mixed numbers, fractions or decimals. Part c uses multiplication by 10 to clear decimal places; the remaining parts use common denominators.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 explains multiplying fractional ratio terms by their lowest common denominator and dividing whole-number terms by their HCF. Page 18 Example 21 demonstrates clearing fractions in mixed-number ratios and then simplifying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear fractional or decimal terms by common multiplication, then reduce the resulting whole-number ratio.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the girls by subtraction, form the ordered boys-to-girls ratio and simplify both terms by a common factor.

questions.mappingNote: Subtract the boys from the school total to obtain the girls, retain boys first in the ratio, and divide both quantities by their highest common factor.
questions.methodNote: Pages 15–16 establish ordered comparisons and finding the remaining part of a whole. Page 17 teaches dividing every ratio term by the highest common factor, demonstrated in Example 19. Page 18 instructs that all Exercise 10D ratios be expressed in simplest form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the number of girls by subtraction, then simplify the boys-to-girls ratio using a common factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate rectangle perimeters and areas before forming and simplifying their ratios.

questions.mappingNote: Each part compares the first rectangle with the second. Parts c and d require calculating perimeter and area before simplifying the resulting ratio; simplification is the common directly assessed ratio skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 compares lengths in a specified order. Page 17 teaches simplifying ratios by dividing all terms by their highest common factor, illustrated in Example 19. Page 18 instructs that all Exercise 10D ratios are to be expressed in simplest form. Rectangle perimeter and area teaching is absent from the supplied evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate rectangle perimeters and areas before forming and simplifying their ratios.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate rectangle perimeters and areas, then simplify comparisons containing decimal measurements.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b compare the first rectangle with the second and simplify. Parts c–d first calculate each perimeter or area and then simplify the comparison. Decimal ratio simplification is the closest listed primary skill; rectangle area is a directly assessed prerequisite.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 compares lengths in the stated order. Page 17 teaches dividing all ratio terms by their HCF; pages 17–18 teach clearing fractional terms before simplifying. The exercise instruction on page 18 requires all ratios in simplest form. Rectangle perimeter and area prerequisite teaching is absent from the supplied evidence.

questions.methodNote: Use the language of equal parts and the unitary method: divide a known quantity by its number of parts, then multiply. Page 15 relates ribbon segment lengths to parts; pages 20–21 explicitly demonstrate finding one part and scaling.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is a practical mixture ratio. The inspected teaching supports parts, component fractions, equivalent ratios and unitary reasoning; repeated removal is an extension requiring independent compatibility review.
questions.methodNote: Use component fractions of a whole, as in Example 16, and simplify fractional ratios as in Examples 20–21. Apply the component fraction to the thoroughly mixed amount removed, then subtract from the component volume and restore the total volume.

classification.difficultyReason: Model both remaining volumes as changing quantities and translate the four-to-one condition into a weighted comparison or equation, rather than comparing drainage rates alone.

questions.mappingNote: Finding the two hourly drainage rates applies the unitary method. Expressing the remaining volumes and equating B to four times A is an authored extension requiring independent taught-method review.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 demonstrates finding and scaling constant rates; pages 15–18 explain ratios and fractions; pages 20–21 develop unitary reasoning using parts. None explicitly demonstrates comparing remaining volumes under unequal drainage.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines component quantities from different mixture ratios and reverses the given ratio order in part c.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts assess practical mixture ratios. Part a combines equal total volumes with different component fractions; part b additionally scales unequal total volumes; part c adds water while preserving concentrate and reverses the given component order. Combining separate mixtures is an extension of the inspected parts method rather than an explicitly demonstrated example.
questions.methodNote: Use total ratio parts to find one part and component volumes, combine like components, then clear fractional denominators and simplify. Pages 15–16 establish mixture parts and fractions of a whole; pages 17–18 simplify fractional ratios; pages 20–21 demonstrate unitary division into parts.
